solution.concept_anchor: Dhar Commission mandate — administrative efficiency over language
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because students frequently conflate the Dhar Commission's conclusion with the later JVP Committee's nuanced deferral, and may recall 'linguistic reorganisation was rejected' without distinguishing which body made which argument.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a) — the JVP Committee, not the Dhar Commission, is the body that deferred linguistic reorganisation conditionally.
Eliminate option (c) — the Dhar Commission preceded the States Reorganisation Commission by five years and had no connection to Fazl Ali.
Eliminate option (d) — the Commission's primary focus was administrative efficiency; equating it with a pro-linguistic stance inverts its actual finding.
Retain option (b) — S.K. Dhar was tasked specifically to evaluate whether administrative efficiency or linguistic affinity should guide reorganisation, and he firmly recommended the former.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap here is entity-swap: students who know 'linguistic reorganisation was rejected early on' may attribute that rejection to the JVP Committee rather than the Dhar Commission, or vice versa. The Dhar Commission's distinguishing feature is that it was constituted on administrative and legal grounds — S.K. Dhar was a retired judge — and its rejection of linguistic basis was unconditional, unlike the JVP's conditional deferral. A partially prepared student conflates both bodies as saying the same thing.
solution.final_explanation:
The Dhar Commission (1948), chaired by retired judge S.K. Dhar, was the first formal post-independence body to examine state reorganisation. Its primary mandate was to assess whether linguistic affinity or administrative efficiency should guide the redrawing of state boundaries.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The JVP Committee, not the Dhar Commission, conditionally deferred linguistic reorganisation. The Dhar Commission's rejection was categorical.
• Option (b) — Correct: S.K. Dhar recommended that administrative convenience and efficiency should be the overriding criterion, explicitly subordinating linguistic considerations.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The Fazl Ali Commission (SRC) was constituted in 1953, five years after the Dhar Commission, and had a distinct multi-factor mandate.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The Dhar Commission did not endorse linguistic reorganisation; it was the first body to formally argue against it.

Value Addition:
• The Dhar Commission report (1948) is distinct from the JVP report (1949) — both rejected linguistic basis but for different reasons.
• S.K. Dhar was a retired judge of the Allahabad High Court, giving the Commission a legal-administrative character.
• Its findings set the political context within which Potti Sriramulu's agitation later forced a reversal.

solution.concept_anchor: JVP Committee composition and conditional deferral

statement_analysis.statement: The JVP Committee included Jawaharlal Nehru, Vallabhbhai Patel, and Pattabhi Sitaramayya.
statement_analysis.reason: The committee was named after its three members: Jawaharlal Nehru (J), Vallabhbhai Patel (V), and Pattabhi Sitaramayya (P) — a Congress Working Committee sub-committee of significant political weight.

statement_analysis.statement: The JVP Committee categorically and permanently rejected the linguistic basis for state reorganisation without any qualification.
statement_analysis.reason: The JVP Committee did NOT permanently reject linguistic reorganisation; it deferred the question conditionally, acknowledging that if sentiments were too strong it might need to be conceded — a nuanced position, not an outright rejection.

statement_analysis.statement: Unlike the Dhar Commission, the JVP Committee was primarily a political body rather than an administrative or legal inquiry.
statement_analysis.reason: The JVP was a sub-committee of the Congress Working Committee composed of senior politicians, whereas the Dhar Commission was headed by a retired judge and had a legal-administrative character.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Selecting all three as correct is the strongest distractor because Statement 2 uses confident language ('categorically and permanently') that superficially matches a student's memory of 'JVP rejected linguistic basis,' without registering the crucial conditional qualifier.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1 — J, V, P acronym maps exactly to Nehru, Patel, Sitaramayya: Correct.
Scrutinise Statement 2 — the word 'permanently' is the trap; JVP left a conditional door open for reorganisation if sentiments proved too strong: Incorrect.
Verify Statement 3 — JVP was a Congress Working Committee sub-committee of politicians, contrasting with Dhar's judicial character: Correct.
Statements 1 and 3 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — select option (c): 1 and 3 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap lies in Statement 2, which adds 'categorically and permanently' to a finding that was actually conditional and temporary. Students who recall 'JVP rejected linguistic basis' without registering the conditional qualifier will mark Statement 2 as correct, leading them to choose 'all three' (option d). The JVP report's actual language acknowledged that if public sentiment proved overwhelming, reorganisation would have to be conceded — a subtle but critical distinction from absolute rejection.
solution.final_explanation:
The JVP Committee (1949) — named for Nehru, Patel, and Pattabhi Sitaramayya — was the Congress Working Committee's response to the Dhar Commission report. It differed from the Dhar Commission in character and conclusion.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The acronym JVP maps precisely to the three members named.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The JVP's rejection was conditional, not permanent. It stated that 'if the sentiment is too strong, we shall have to concede it' — leaving the door open, which was precisely what Nehru walked through after Potti Sriramulu's death in 1952.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The JVP was a political sub-committee of the Congress Working Committee, giving its deliberations a political rather than technocratic character.

Value Addition:
• 'P' in JVP refers to Pattabhi Sitaramayya, not Purushottam Das Tandon — a common name-confusion trap.
• The JVP's conditional deferral became politically untenable after 1952, showing the limits of elite consensus against mass agitation.
• This makes JVP significant not for what it decided but for what it left undecided.

solution.concept_anchor: Andhra State 1953 distinct from Andhra Pradesh 1956

statement_analysis.statement: Andhra State, carved out of Madras State in 1953, was the first state in independent India formed primarily on the basis of linguistic identity.
statement_analysis.reason: Andhra State was indeed formed in October 1953 after Potti Sriramulu's 58-day fast-unto-death, making it the first linguistic state — this statement is factually accurate.

statement_analysis.statement: Andhra Pradesh, formed under the States Reorganisation Act 1956, comprised the same territory as Andhra State with only minor boundary adjustments.
statement_analysis.reason: Andhra Pradesh in 1956 incorporated the Telangana region from the former Hyderabad state — a substantial addition that included major territory, not a minor boundary adjustment. This merger was governed by the Gentlemen's Agreement 1956.

statement_analysis.statement: Potti Sriramulu undertook his fast in support of a demand for a separate Telugu-speaking state to be separated from the then composite Madras State.
statement_analysis.reason: Sriramulu's fast-unto-death was specifically to agitate for a Telugu-speaking Andhra carved from Madras State — factually accurate.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) lists Statements 2 and 3 as incorrect; a student who misremembers Sriramulu's fast as being for a composite Telugu state including Hyderabad territories might reject Statement 3, making option (c) attractive.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1 — Andhra State, October 1953, first linguistic state: this is correct, so it cannot be the answer.
Evaluate Statement 2 — 'minor boundary adjustments' is the trap phrase; Telangana from Hyderabad was a massive territorial addition: this is INCORRECT.
Evaluate Statement 3 — Sriramulu's demand was specifically for Telugu speakers in Madras State: this is correct, so it cannot be the answer.
Only Statement 2 is incorrect — select option (b): 2 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap in Statement 2 conflates the 1953 Andhra State with the 1956 Andhra Pradesh. Students who know both events often assume they are the same entity with slight modifications. The critical distinction is that Andhra Pradesh 1956 included the entire Telangana region from Hyderabad — a politically charged, historically separate territory — making it fundamentally different from Andhra State 1953, not just a boundary-adjusted version of it.
solution.final_explanation:
The formation of Andhra State (1953) and Andhra Pradesh (1956) are two distinct events that students frequently collapse into one.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Andhra State, formed in October 1953 following Potti Sriramulu's 58-day fast and death, was India's first state carved on linguistic lines.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Andhra Pradesh (1956) included the Telangana region from the former Hyderabad state — a substantial merger, not a minor adjustment. This union was politically negotiated through the Gentlemen's Agreement 1956.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Sriramulu's agitation was directed at Madras State, demanding separation of its Telugu-speaking districts.

Value Addition:
• Sriramulu's 58-day fast ended with his death on 15 December 1952; Andhra State was announced in October 1953.
• The Telangana merger created internal tensions that eventually led to the Jai Telangana movement (1969) and Telangana state (2014).
• The Gentlemen's Agreement 1956 governing the merger was a political compact, not a constitutional provision — a recurring UPSC theme.

solution.concept_anchor: SRC four-factor framework and multi-factor mandate

statement_analysis.statement: The States Reorganisation Commission (1953) was constituted solely to recommend the reorganisation of states on linguistic lines.
statement_analysis.reason: The SRC had a broader mandate — it was asked to undertake a comprehensive review of state reorganisation considering multiple factors including language, geography, economic viability, and administrative convenience.

statement_analysis.statement: H.N. Kunzru and K.M. Panikkar were members of the States Reorganisation Commission along with Chairman Fazl Ali.
statement_analysis.reason: The three-member SRC comprised Fazl Ali (Chairman), Hriday Nath Kunzru, and K.M. Panikkar — this is the correct composition.

statement_analysis.statement: The SRC's framework included preservation of national unity and security as one of its criteria alongside linguistic homogeneity.
statement_analysis.reason: The four-factor framework explicitly placed preservation of India's unity and security as the first criterion, preceding linguistic and cultural homogeneity.

statement_analysis.statement: The SRC endorsed the principle of 'one language–one state' as the foundational rule for reorganisation.
statement_analysis.reason: The SRC explicitly rejected the 'one language–one state' formula, acknowledging India's multilingual realities and treating language as an important but not exclusive criterion.

solution.strong_distractor: c — 'Only three' is the strongest distractor because Statement 1 contains a plausible half-truth (language was clearly the dominant consideration in practice) and a student who reads carelessly may assume the SRC's mandate included only linguistic reorganisation.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1 — 'solely' for linguistic lines is the trap word; the SRC had a multi-factor mandate: Incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 2 — Fazl Ali, Kunzru, Panikkar is the verified composition: Correct.
Evaluate Statement 3 — national unity and security was the first of four criteria in the SRC framework: Correct.
Evaluate Statement 4 — 'one language–one state' was explicitly rejected by the SRC: Incorrect.
Only Statements 2 and 3 are correct — select option (b): Only two.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The partial-truth trap operates in Statement 1: the SRC's work is popularly associated with linguistic reorganisation, making 'solely for linguistic lines' feel plausible. However, the Commission's actual mandate was explicitly multi-factor. Similarly, Statement 4 exploits the common assumption that because the 1956 Act is called 'linguistic reorganisation,' the SRC must have endorsed a one-language-one-state formula — it did the opposite.
solution.final_explanation:
The States Reorganisation Commission (1953–55), chaired by Fazl Ali with H.N. Kunzru and K.M. Panikkar, is frequently mischaracterised as a purely linguistic reorganisation exercise.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: 'Solely' linguistic lines is wrong; the SRC had a four-factor mandate covering national unity, linguistic homogeneity, economic viability, and administrative convenience.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Fazl Ali, Kunzru, and Panikkar is the verified three-member composition.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Preservation of unity and security was the primary criterion, placed ahead of linguistic considerations in the SRC's own framework.
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: The SRC explicitly rejected the 'one language–one state' formula, recognising India's multilingual realities.

Value Addition:
• K.M. Panikkar was a diplomat-historian, giving the SRC diplomatic and historical sensitivity alongside administrative expertise.
• The SRC submitted its report in 1955; the Act followed in 1956.
• The SRC's multi-factor approach is why states like Bombay were kept bilingual initially — the formula was deliberately flexible.

States Reorganisation Act 1956: Key Constitutional Amendments Enabling It

solution.concept_anchor: Pre-1956 four-part state classification — Part A, B, C, D
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) swaps Part B and Part C, which many students confuse because both involve non-Governor's province territories; the distinction between 'former princely states' (B) and 'centrally administered territories' (C) is frequently mixed up.
elimination_logic: Anchor on Part D — Andaman & Nicobar Islands as the sole Part D territory is a well-known fact; any option that reassigns it is wrong: eliminates options with D incorrectly placed.
Recall that Part A states were former Governor's provinces of British India — directly administered; this confirms A–1 pairing.
Part B states were former princely states that had acceded and been integrated — Hyderabad, Mysore, Travancore-Cochin; confirms B–3.
Part C states were centrally administered territories like Coorg, Delhi, Ajmer-Merwara; confirms C–2, and the correct answer is option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap targets the Part B / Part C distinction. Students who vaguely remember 'princely states were Part B' may hesitate when they see 'centrally administered territories' labelled Part C, as both feel like they belong in a similar administrative category. The trap option (b) reverses B and C, which is the single most common error students make on this topic.
solution.final_explanation:
Before the 7th Constitutional Amendment Act 1956 and the States Reorganisation Act 1956, Indian states were classified into four categories based on their administrative origins.

Correct pairings: A–1 (Governor's provinces), B–3 (former princely states), C–2 (centrally administered territories), D–4 (Andaman & Nicobar).

The trap pairings in wrong options swap B and C. Part B states — including Hyderabad, Mysore, and Travancore-Cochin — had Rajpramukhs (ex-rulers) who were replaced by Governors after 1956, achieving democratic uniformity. Part C states were directly administered by the Centre through a Chief Commissioner.

The 7th Constitutional Amendment abolished this four-part system, creating a binary of States and Union Territories.

Value Addition:
• Rajpramukhs were abolished in 1956 — a significant step in completing the integration of princely states into India's democratic framework.
• Coorg (Kodagu) was a Part C state before being merged into Mysore under SRA 1956.
• Delhi was also a Part C state — it only became a Union Territory with special powers (NCT) much later under the 69th Amendment (1991).

concepts_used: Role of Article 3 in Post-1956 Reorganisations: Parliament's Plenary Power
States Reorganisation Act 1956: Key Constitutional Amendments Enabling It

solution.concept_anchor: Article 3 — consultation not concurrence for state reorganisation
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who correctly identify both A and R as true may assume R explains A, missing the crucial distinction that Parliament's power under Article 3 does not derive from the absence of a requirement for special majority but from the constitutional design that treats reorganisation as a legislative function.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Parliament can redraw state boundaries through ordinary legislation under Article 3 without requiring state consent: Yes, A is correct.
Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — The Babulal Parate case (1960) did uphold Parliament's plenary power under Article 3: Yes, R is correct.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — The Babulal Parate case confirmed the constitutional position but did not create or cause Parliament's power; the power derives from the text of Article 3 itself, not from a judicial ruling. R is an affirmation of A, not its explanation.
Both A and R are correct but R does not causally explain A — correct option is (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The reversed-causation trap: students see two true statements and instinctively mark (a). But the Babulal Parate judgment affirmed Parliament's power; it did not create or cause it. The power under Article 3 is textual and constitutional — the Supreme Court's ruling is confirmatory, not explanatory. This is a classic UPSC assertion-reason trap where both facts are true but the causal arrow runs from the Constitution to the judgment, not from the judgment to Parliament's power.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 3 of the Indian Constitution grants Parliament the power to form new states, increase or diminish the area of states, alter state boundaries, and change state names — all through ordinary legislation (simple majority), not a constitutional amendment.

Assertion (A) is correct: Parliament has plenary power under Article 3, requiring only consultation with (not concurrence of) the affected state legislature.

Reason (R) is correct: The Supreme Court in Babulal Parate v. State of Bombay (1960) upheld Parliament's power, holding that Article 3 did not require the affected state's consent.

However, R does not explain A causally. Parliament's power under Article 3 derives from the constitutional text itself, not from the Babulal Parate judgment. The judgment confirmed what the Constitution already said.

Value Addition:
• The distinction between 'consultation' and 'concurrence' under Article 3 is a high-frequency UPSC conceptual trap.
• Telangana's creation in 2014 illustrated this — Andhra Pradesh legislature passed a negative resolution, which Parliament validly overrode.
• Article 3 reorganisation is by ordinary majority; Article 368 constitutional amendments require special majority — an important structural distinction.

concepts_used: Bombay Reorganisation Act 1960: Maharashtra–Gujarat Bifurcation and Samyukta Maharashtra/Mahagujarat Movements

solution.concept_anchor: Bombay reorganisation — SRC recommendation to Act 1960 sequence
solution.strong_distractor: a — Placing the SRC recommendation and the Bombay Reorganisation Act in the same period (both as 1956 events) is the strongest trap for students who know the Act is 'post-SRA' but cannot recall that the SRC actually recommended a bilingual Bombay in 1955.
elimination_logic: The SRC (Fazl Ali Commission) submitted its report in 1955, before the States Reorganisation Act — this must come first.
The States Reorganisation Act 1956 implemented modified SRC recommendations but kept Bombay bilingual — this is the second event.
The Samyukta Maharashtra and Mahagujarat agitations intensified after the 1956 Act rejected immediate bifurcation — this precedes the 1960 resolution.
The Bombay Reorganisation Act 1960 finally bifurcated the state into Maharashtra and Gujarat — this is last. Correct sequence: 1-3-4-2, which corresponds to option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap: students know the SRC report (1955), the SRA (1956), and the Bombay Act (1960) but frequently misplace the agitations — assuming they preceded rather than followed the SRC's recommendation. The agitations intensified as a reaction to the SRC's bilingual Bombay proposal, not before it.
solution.final_explanation:
The Bombay question unfolded over a decade, making chronology a natural testing ground.

Correct sequence:
1. SRC submits report recommending a bilingual Bombay state (1955)
2. States Reorganisation Act 1956 retains Bombay as a bilingual state
3. Samyukta Maharashtra and Mahagujarat agitations intensify against the bilingual arrangement
4. Bombay Reorganisation Act 1960 bifurcates Bombay into Maharashtra and Gujarat

Wrong options fail by:
— Placing the agitations before the SRC report (they were a reaction to it)
— Treating the Bombay Act as part of the 1956 reorganisation (it came four years later)
— Reversing steps 2 and 3 (the Act preceded the peak of the agitations' political success)

Value Addition:
• Bombay city was initially proposed as a separate Union Territory — political resistance from both communities ended this idea.
• Maharashtra Day and Gujarat Day are both celebrated on 1 May — the date of the 1960 bifurcation.
• The Bombay question is the clearest evidence that SRA 1956 was not the final settlement of linguistic reorganisation.

Mahajan Commission 1966: Maharashtra–Karnataka Border Dispute and Its Non-Implementation

solution.concept_anchor: Shah Commission vs Mahajan Commission — 1966 parallel commissions
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who recall 'Mahajan Commission was 1966 and dealt with Punjab' will confidently choose option (b), conflating the Shah Commission (Punjab) with the Mahajan Commission (Maharashtra-Karnataka) — both from 1966.
elimination_logic: The scenario describes a Marathi-speaking border town claimed by both Maharashtra and Karnataka — this maps to the Maharashtra-Karnataka border dispute, not the Punjab-Haryana situation.
Eliminate option (a) — the SRC 1956 dealt with the initial reorganisation, not post-1956 boundary disputes between states.
Eliminate option (b) — Shah Commission 1966 was constituted for Punjab's bifurcation into Punjab and Haryana, not for Maharashtra-Karnataka borders.
Eliminate option (c) — Sarkaria Commission examined Centre-State relations broadly, not a specific inter-state boundary dispute.
Retain option (d) — the Mahajan Commission (1966) was specifically constituted to adjudicate the Maharashtra-Karnataka border dispute including Belgaum/Belagavi.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap: both the Shah Commission and the Mahajan Commission were constituted in 1966, creating a strong conflation risk. Students who know 'there was a commission in 1966 for reorganisation' without distinguishing the two will conflate Shah (Punjab-Haryana) with Mahajan (Maharashtra-Karnataka). The scenario's reference to Marathi-speaking pockets in Karnataka is the distinguishing detail that points unambiguously to the Mahajan Commission.
solution.final_explanation:
Following the 1956 reorganisation, linguistic minorities emerged as a persistent problem — Marathi-speaking pockets in Karnataka and Kannada-speaking areas in Maharashtra created a live border dispute. The scenario describes a Marathi-speaking town within Karnataka's territory — the classic Belgaum (Belagavi) scenario.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The SRC completed its work in 1955; it was not the mechanism for post-1956 inter-state disputes.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: The Shah Commission (1966) addressed Punjab's bifurcation into Punjab and Haryana on linguistic lines — an entirely different dispute.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The Sarkaria Commission (1983-87) examined broad Centre-State relations, not a specific border dispute between two states.
• Option (d) — Correct: The Mahajan Commission (1966) was constituted specifically to resolve the Maharashtra-Karnataka border dispute, particularly regarding Belgaum and surrounding Marathi-speaking areas. Maharashtra rejected its findings, leaving the dispute unresolved.

Value Addition:
• The Mahajan Commission awarded the majority of disputed areas to Karnataka — its report was never formally implemented.
• Belagavi remains a live political issue; Karnataka holds its winter session of the legislature there symbolically.
• Both 1966 commissions — Shah (Punjab) and Mahajan (Maharashtra-Karnataka) — are recurring UPSC trap pairings.

concepts_used: Nagaland (1963) and North-East Reorganisation: Ethnicity vs. Language as Reorganisation Basis

solution.concept_anchor: Nagaland — ethnic/tribal basis, exception to linguistic principle
solution.strong_distractor: b — Meghalaya (1972) is a strong distractor because students may know it was also created for tribal/ethnic reasons and assume it belongs with the 'exceptions,' forgetting that the question asks which was the FIRST and most explicit statutory exception to the linguistic principle.
elimination_logic: Identify the grouping principle — the question concerns the basis of state formation: linguistic vs. ethnic/tribal.
Kerala (1956), Karnataka (1956), and Andhra Pradesh (1956) were all formed under the States Reorganisation Act on linguistic lines — they share the linguistic basis.
Nagaland (1963) was carved out on ethnic/tribal grounds (Naga tribal identity), not on the basis of a shared language — it is the structural exception.
Nagaland does not share the linguistic basis attribute with the other three — it is the odd one out. Correct option: (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap: students who know 'Nagaland is different' may still pick Meghalaya (option b) if they believe Meghalaya is the stronger example of tribal-based reorganisation, overlooking that Meghalaya (1972) is not listed. The key is that all three other options — Kerala, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh — share the linguistic basis of the 1956 Act, making Nagaland the clear structural outlier. The trap works by making students second-guess whether Nagaland is 'different enough.'
solution.final_explanation:
The question tests knowledge of the basis on which different Indian states were formed.

• Option (a) Kerala — formed in 1956 under SRA on the linguistic basis (Malayalam-speaking merger of Travancore-Cochin and Malabar).
• Option (b) Karnataka (then Mysore) — formed in 1956 under SRA on the linguistic basis (Kannada-speaking consolidation).
• Option (c) Nagaland — formed in 1963 on ethnic/tribal grounds (Naga tribal identity), making it a deliberate exception to the linguistic principle. It does NOT share the linguistic basis with the others.
• Option (d) Andhra Pradesh — formed in 1956 under SRA on the linguistic basis (Telugu-speaking merger of Andhra State and Telangana).

Value Addition:
• Nagaland's statehood was preceded by the 16-Point Agreement (1960) between the Government of India and Naga People's Convention.
• Nagaland became a full state on 1 December 1963 — India's 16th state.
• The North-East (Meghalaya, Manipur, Tripura — 1972) followed Nagaland's ethnic/tribal template, creating a North-East exception to the 1956 linguistic principle.

solution.concept_anchor: Gentlemen's Agreement 1956 — political compact, not constitutional provision

statement_analysis.statement: The Gentlemen's Agreement of 1956 was a formal constitutional provision incorporated into the Constitution to safeguard Telangana's interests in the merged Andhra Pradesh state.
statement_analysis.reason: The Gentlemen's Agreement was a political understanding between Andhra and Telangana leaders — it was never incorporated into the Constitution or given statutory force, which is precisely why it was so easily eroded in subsequent years.

statement_analysis.statement: The Mulki Rules, which restricted government employment in Telangana to those with a defined period of residence in the region, were a key element of the safeguards that the Gentlemen's Agreement sought to protect.
statement_analysis.reason: Mulki Rules (requiring local residency for public employment in Telangana) were a core safeguard under the Gentlemen's Agreement and their erosion triggered the Jai Telangana movement of 1969.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) (both correct) is deceptive because students who know the Gentlemen's Agreement 'had constitutional significance' may assume its provisions were constitutionally entrenched, when in fact it was merely a political compact.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1 — 'formal constitutional provision' is the trap phrase; the Gentlemen's Agreement was a political understanding, never constitutionally incorporated: Incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 2 — Mulki Rules as a residency-based employment safeguard under the Agreement is factually established: Correct.
Statement 1 Incorrect + Statement 2 Correct maps to option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap in Statement 1 adds 'formal constitutional provision incorporated into the Constitution' to a fact that students recall as 'important safeguard for Telangana.' The critical distinction is the Agreement's non-constitutional nature — it was a political compact, which is exactly why it was violated without legal consequence. Students who know the Agreement was significant but not its legal form will mark it as constitutional.
solution.final_explanation:
The Gentlemen's Agreement (1956) was negotiated between Andhra and Telangana political leaders as a condition for the merger into Andhra Pradesh. Its non-constitutional character is its most legally significant feature.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The Agreement was a political compact, not a constitutional provision. It was never embedded in the Constitution or given statutory force — this is the root cause of its subsequent erosion and the Telangana agitation.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The Mulki Rules, requiring a defined period of residence in Telangana for government employment, were a key protective mechanism under the Agreement. Their perceived erosion sparked the Jai Telangana movement (1969) and the Telangana Praja Samithi's political agitation.

Value Addition:
• The Gentlemen's Agreement also provided for a regional committee for Telangana and proportional representation in educational institutions.
• The Supreme Court upheld the validity of Mulki Rules in 1972, but the political response was turbulent.
• The failure of the Gentlemen's Agreement is the direct historical predecessor to the demand for separate Telangana state, ultimately achieved in 2014.

solution.concept_anchor: Telangana 2014 — bifurcation of linguistically homogeneous state
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who recall 'Parliament needs state concurrence for reorganisation' will select 'with the concurrence of the Andhra Pradesh legislature,' inverting the actual constitutional requirement of consultation only.
elimination_logic: Article 3 requires only consultation with the state legislature, not concurrence — eliminating option (a).
The Andhra Pradesh legislature passed a negative resolution against bifurcation — Parliament proceeded anyway, confirming option (b).
Eliminate option (c) — a constitutional amendment under Article 368 was not required; reorganisation is ordinary legislation under Article 3.
Eliminate option (d) — the President's reference to the Supreme Court is not required under Article 3; the question describes a different procedure.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap: students who know 'Parliament must consult the state' may extend that to 'Parliament must have the state's agreement,' inverting the constitutional position. The Telangana case is the most dramatic recent illustration that consultation is all that is required — the Andhra Pradesh legislature's explicit opposition did not prevent Parliament from proceeding.
solution.final_explanation:
The Telangana case (2014) is the most instructive modern application of Article 3.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Parliament does not need concurrence; only consultation is required under Article 3. The Andhra Pradesh legislature actively opposed bifurcation.
• Option (b) — Correct: Parliament proceeded with the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act 2014 after consulting (not obtaining consent from) the state legislature, which had passed a resolution against it.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: A constitutional amendment under Article 368 was not needed; Article 3 allows reorganisation through ordinary legislation.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: No presidential reference to the Supreme Court is required under Article 3 for state reorganisation.

Value Addition:
• Telangana became India's 29th state on 2 June 2014.
• Hyderabad was designated as the shared capital of Telangana and Andhra Pradesh for up to 10 years.
• Telangana's formation contradicted the 1956 premise — linguistic unity of Telugu speakers was the justification for merger; that same unity was now deemed insufficient to prevent separation.

solution.concept_anchor: Kerala formation — Travancore-Cochin and Malabar merger
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who recall 'Andhra Pradesh = Andhra + something from Hyderabad' may accept 'Rayalaseema' as the Hyderabad contribution, when in fact it was the Telangana region that came from Hyderabad state.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a) — Andhra Pradesh was formed by merging Andhra State with the Telangana region of Hyderabad, not Rayalaseema (which was already part of Andhra State).
Eliminate option (b) — Karnataka (then Mysore) was formed by merging territories from multiple states including Bombay, Hyderabad, and Madras — it was not a simple Mysore-Coorg merger alone.
Evaluate option (c) — Kerala was formed by merging Travancore-Cochin with the Malayalam-speaking Malabar district from Madras State: this is the correct pairing.
Eliminate option (d) — Maharashtra was formed from Bombay State after the 1960 bifurcation, not directly from Hyderabad territories.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The geographic-swap trap in option (a) substitutes Rayalaseema (which was part of Andhra State) for Telangana (which came from Hyderabad). Rayalaseema is a Telugu-speaking region of the original Andhra State and sounds plausible as a Hyderabad contribution because students vaguely recall 'Telugu territory from Hyderabad.' The precise answer is that Telangana (not Rayalaseema) was the Hyderabad contribution to Andhra Pradesh.
solution.final_explanation:
The 1956 reorganisation involved complex multi-state mergers, and getting the precise territorial contributions right is a common UPSC discriminator.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Andhra Pradesh was formed by merging Andhra State with the Telangana region of Hyderabad, not Rayalaseema. Rayalaseema was already part of Andhra State before 1956.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Karnataka (Mysore) was a multi-source merger including parts of Bombay, Hyderabad, and Madras states along with Mysore and Coorg — not merely Mysore and Coorg.
• Option (c) — Correct: Kerala was formed by merging Travancore-Cochin (a Part B state) with the Malabar district (from Madras State) — both Malayalam-speaking territories.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Maharashtra was formed from Bombay State under the Bombay Reorganisation Act 1960, not from Hyderabad territories.

Value Addition:
• Coorg (Kodagu) was a Part C state merged into Mysore/Karnataka — not into Kerala or Andhra.
• The Malayalam-speaking Kasaragod area was transferred from Madras to Kerala — a sub-district level adjustment.
• Malabar district's inclusion in Kerala is the origin of the distinct Malabar cultural sub-region within Kerala.

solution.concept_anchor: 2000 states — regional/tribal basis, not linguistic

statement_analysis.statement: All three states formed in November 2000 — Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, and Uttarakhand — were created primarily on the basis of regional, developmental, or tribal identity rather than a distinct linguistic identity.
statement_analysis.reason: Jharkhand (tribal identity and resource exploitation), Chhattisgarh (regional development argument), and Uttarakhand (hill-plains administrative divide) were all formed on non-linguistic grounds, marking a clear evolution from the 1956 linguistic principle.

statement_analysis.statement: The linguistic basis for state reorganisation established in 1956 was constitutionally entrenched in Article 3, making it mandatory for all future reorganisations to follow the linguistic criterion.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 3 does not mandate any particular criterion for reorganisation — it merely empowers Parliament to reorganise states. The linguistic principle was a policy choice of the 1956 Act, not a constitutional requirement.

statement_analysis.statement: The formation of Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, and Uttarakhand demonstrated that the criteria for state reorganisation could evolve beyond the framework set by the States Reorganisation Act 1956.
statement_analysis.reason: The 2000 reorganisations explicitly departed from the linguistic template, showing that Article 3's flexibility allowed Parliament to apply different criteria in different historical contexts.

solution.strong_distractor: d — All three correct is the strong distractor because Statement 2 uses authoritative-sounding language ('constitutionally entrenched') that students who conflate constitutional provisions with policy decisions may accept.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1 — Jharkhand (tribal), Chhattisgarh (developmental), Uttarakhand (hill-plains): all non-linguistic basis: Correct.
Interrogate Statement 2 — Article 3 is a power provision, not a criteria-mandating provision; linguistic basis was policy, not constitutional mandate: Incorrect.
Verify Statement 3 — 2000 reorganisations explicitly followed non-linguistic logic, confirming criteria evolution: Correct.
Statements 1 and 3 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — select option (a): 1 and 3 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The partial-truth trap in Statement 2 exploits the widespread assumption that because 1956 Act is famous for the 'linguistic principle,' it must have embedded that principle in the Constitution. In reality, the linguistic principle was a policy decision of Parliament in 1956 — Article 3 itself is criterion-neutral. Students who confuse constitutional entrenchment with legislative precedent will mark Statement 2 as correct.
solution.final_explanation:
The 2000 reorganisations represent a significant evolution in India's approach to state formation.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Jharkhand (tribal identity and historical exploitation of mineral-rich regions), Chhattisgarh (regional development and administrative autonomy for a backward region), and Uttarakhand (distinctive hill culture and governance needs) were all formed on non-linguistic grounds.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Article 3 is a procedural/power provision — it says Parliament CAN reorganise states but specifies no criteria. The linguistic principle of 1956 was a policy choice, not constitutionally mandated. This is why Parliament could freely apply different criteria in 2000.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The 2000 reorganisations demonstrate the flexibility of Article 3, allowing Parliament to respond to regional aspirations beyond the linguistic template.

Value Addition:
• All three states were formed on 1 November 2000 (Chhattisgarh and Madhya Pradesh) — actually Chhattisgarh was 1 Nov, Uttarakhand 9 Nov, Jharkhand 15 Nov 2000.
• Jharkhand was carved from Bihar, Chhattisgarh from Madhya Pradesh, Uttarakhand from Uttar Pradesh.
• These formations showed that development deficit and sub-regional identity could be independent grounds for statehood.

concepts_used: Sarkaria Commission (1983–87) and Inter-State Council on Reorganisation Demands: Centre–State Dimension

solution.concept_anchor: Sarkaria Commission recommendation vs Inter-State Council establishment — time gap

statement_analysis.statement: The Sarkaria Commission (1983–87) examined Centre-State relations and recommended the establishment of a permanent Inter-State Council under Article 263.
statement_analysis.reason: The Sarkaria Commission, constituted in 1983 and reporting in 1987, examined Centre-State relations comprehensively and specifically recommended a permanent Inter-State Council as a dispute resolution mechanism including for boundary disputes.

statement_analysis.statement: The Inter-State Council was established in 1983, the same year the Sarkaria Commission was constituted, acting simultaneously as the mechanism to implement the Commission's terms of reference.
statement_analysis.reason: The Inter-State Council was established in 1990, three years after the Sarkaria Commission submitted its report — not in 1983. The time gap between recommendation and implementation is a recurring UPSC trap.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 263 of the Constitution provides the constitutional basis for the establishment of the Inter-State Council.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 263 empowers the President to establish an Inter-State Council if it appears necessary for the public interest — this is the constitutional basis on which the Inter-State Council was established by Presidential Order in 1990.

statement_analysis.statement: The Sarkaria Commission highlighted that ad hoc state reorganisation without a systemic mechanism creates long-term federal tensions.
statement_analysis.reason: This was a core observation of the Sarkaria Commission — that India's pattern of responding to reorganisation demands on a crisis-by-crisis basis, without a permanent forum for inter-state disputes, exacerbated federal tensions.

solution.strong_distractor: c — 'Only three' is tempting because Statement 2's false claim about 1983 is easy to overlook if a student remembers only that 'Sarkaria Commission and Inter-State Council are connected,' assuming the Council was established alongside the Commission.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1 — Sarkaria Commission (1983-87) recommending Inter-State Council under Article 263: established fact: Correct.
Evaluate Statement 2 — 'established in 1983' is the trap; the Inter-State Council was established in 1990, three years post-report: Incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 3 — Article 263 as the constitutional basis of the Inter-State Council: textually verifiable: Correct.
Evaluate Statement 4 — Sarkaria's observation on ad hoc reorganisation and federal tensions: documented finding: Correct.
Three statements correct, one incorrect — select option (c): Only three.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap in Statement 2 places the Inter-State Council's establishment in 1983 — the year the Sarkaria Commission was constituted — rather than 1990, when it was actually established. Students who associate the Commission with the Council without tracking the three-year implementation gap will accept 1983 as plausible. This is a precision-recall trap of the kind UPSC deploys for institutional timelines.
solution.final_explanation:
The Sarkaria Commission (1983–87) is a pivotal body in Centre-State relations and its connection to the Inter-State Council tests precision recall.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Sarkaria Commission did recommend a permanent Inter-State Council under Article 263.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The Inter-State Council was established in 1990 by Presidential Order, three years after the Commission's 1987 report — not in 1983.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Article 263 is the constitutional basis; the President may establish the Council when it appears necessary in the public interest.
• Statement 4 — Correct: Sarkaria's systemic critique of ad hoc reorganisation is a documented finding of the Commission.

Three correct, one incorrect — option (c).

Value Addition:
• The Inter-State Council was reconstituted in 2016 and again in 2023 — its periodic reconstitution is itself a UPSC-relevant fact.
• The Punchhi Commission (2007–10) further examined Centre-State relations, building on Sarkaria's framework.
• Article 263 also enables coordination councils for common subjects — distinct from the dispute resolution function.

solution.concept_anchor: Constitutional articles for linguistic minorities — Article 347, 350A
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) swaps Article 347 and Article 350A, which students frequently confuse because both deal with linguistic minorities but at different levels of governance and through different mechanisms.
elimination_logic: Anchor on Article 350A — 'instruction in mother tongue at primary level' is a specific and recalled fact: confirms A–3 is wrong pairing; A should map to 347.
Article 347 deals with the President's power to direct official recognition of a regional language — distinct from primary education instruction: confirms A–2.
Article 350A specifically mandates adequate facilities for instruction in the mother tongue at primary stage for linguistic minority children: confirms B–3.

Article 350B established the office of Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities (Commissioner): confirms C–1. Article 29 protects cultural and educational rights of minorities broadly: confirms D–4. Correct answer: option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap targets Article 347 and Article 350A, which both deal with linguistic minorities but address different mechanisms: Article 347 is about presidential recognition of regional languages for official use, while Article 350A is specifically about primary education in the mother tongue. Students who conflate these two articles will select option (b), which swaps them.
solution.final_explanation:
Articles 347, 350A, and 350B form a trio of constitutional provisions protecting linguistic minorities — a direct consequence of the 1956 reorganisation creating new linguistic minority communities.

Correct pairings: A (Article 347) – 2 (President may direct official recognition of a regional language if a substantial proportion speaks it), B (Article 350A) – 3 (facilities for instruction in mother tongue at primary stage for linguistic minority children), C (Article 350B) – 1 (Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities appointed by President), D (Article 29) – 4 (minorities' right to conserve distinct language, script, and culture).

The trap pairing in wrong options confuses 347 and 350A. Article 347 is about language recognition at the official/state level; Article 350A is specifically about primary education.

Value Addition:
• The Commissioner for Linguistic Minorities (Article 350B) reports to the President and submits reports that are laid before Parliament.
• Belagavi (Belgaum) dispute between Maharashtra and Karnataka is the most prominent Article 347-related live issue.
• Article 29 protects minority rights broadly; Article 30 adds the right to establish and administer educational institutions — often tested together.

solution.concept_anchor: Nehru's pragmatic reversal — political compulsion over ideological conviction
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Nehru's post-independence caution about linguistic reorganisation, shaped by Partition trauma, is documented — he feared it would fragment the nation: Yes, A is correct.
Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — Nehru had indeed supported linguistic provinces in the 1928 Nehru Report: Yes, R is correct.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — Nehru's post-independence caution was NOT caused by his 1928 support; his 1928 position was pro-linguistic. The caution arose from Partition trauma and post-1947 nation-building anxieties — a separate and later cause. The 1928 support and the post-1947 caution are in tension, not causal sequence.
Both A and R are correct but R does not explain A — the causal arrow is absent. Correct option is (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The reversed-causation trap: students see 'Nehru's past position' and 'Nehru's later position' and assume the earlier position explains the later one — as if continuity of thought explains change. But Nehru's post-independence caution was caused by Partition trauma (1947), not by his 1928 support. In fact, the 1928 and post-1947 positions are opposites, making R true but causally irrelevant to A.
solution.final_explanation:
Nehru's evolving position on linguistic reorganisation is one of India's most instructive cases of political pragmatism overcoming ideological consistency.

Assertion (A) is correct: Nehru's post-independence caution about linguistic reorganisation was genuine and rooted in the trauma of Partition — he feared that dividing India on linguistic lines would replay the communal fragmentation of 1947.

Reason (R) is correct: The 1928 Nehru Report did support the principle of linguistic provinces in the context of reorganising British India — Nehru of 1928 was pro-linguistic reorganisation.

However, R does not explain A. The 1928 position and the post-1947 caution are causally disconnected. The caution arose from Partition's lessons, not from the 1928 stance. They are in tension — Nehru reversed himself. His 1953 concession (after Sriramulu's death) was driven by political compulsion, not by a return to 1928 thinking.

Value Addition:
• Nehru called Potti Sriramulu's death a 'tragic event' and announced Andhra State within days — demonstrating political compulsion's primacy.
• The 'unity in diversity' framework allowed Nehru to later reframe linguistic states as strengthening, not threatening, national unity.
• Nehru's evolution on this issue is a model of how elite ideological positions yield to mass democratic pressures.

solution.concept_anchor: Coorg — Part C state, viability criterion, merged into Mysore 1956
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who recall 'Coorg was merged into Kerala' will select option (a), confusing the Malayalam-adjacent geography of Coorg with its actual administrative destination of Mysore/Karnataka.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a) — Coorg was merged into Mysore (Karnataka), not Kerala; Malabar district was the Malayalam-speaking region that went to Kerala.
Eliminate option (b) — Coorg was a Part C state (centrally administered), not a Part B state (former princely state with Rajpramukh).
Eliminate option (d) — the SRC's viability criterion worked against Coorg's independent statehood; the SRC did not support retaining Coorg as a separate unit.
Retain option (c) — Coorg was a Part C state before 1956, merged into Mysore under SRA 1956 because it was deemed too small to be economically or administratively viable as an independent state.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap substitutes Kerala for Mysore/Karnataka as the destination of Coorg's merger. Students familiar with Coorg's location in the Western Ghats near Kerala may geographically associate it with Kerala. However, Coorg (Kodagu) was merged into Mysore on the basis of Kannada-speaking population dominance and geographical contiguity with Mysore, not proximity to Kerala.
solution.final_explanation:
Coorg (Kodagu) exemplifies how the SRC applied the economic viability criterion to override local identity claims.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Coorg was merged into Mysore (now Karnataka), not Kerala. The Malabar district from Madras State was the territory that went to Kerala.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Coorg was a Part C state — centrally administered — not a Part B state. Part B states were former princely states with Rajpramukhs.
• Option (c) — Correct: Coorg was a Part C state before 1956 and was merged into Mysore (Karnataka) under the SRA 1956, as the SRC determined it was too small to be economically or administratively viable as an independent state.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The SRC applied the viability criterion to conclude that Coorg could not stand alone — this was the reason for merger, not a reason to retain independence.

Value Addition:
• Coorg/Kodagu is a hill district in Karnataka known for coffee cultivation and the Kodava people.
• The viability criterion from the SRC continues to be cited in debates about demands for small states.
• Kodagu periodically sees demands for separate statehood — a live political issue invoking the same identity arguments the SRC overrode in 1956.

solution.concept_anchor: Sequence: Dhar Commission → JVP Committee → SRC → SRA
solution.strong_distractor: a — Placing the JVP Committee before the Dhar Commission is the strongest trap because students who remember 'JVP was the more politically significant body' may rank it first, not recalling that the Dhar Commission was the earlier and more administrative precursor.
elimination_logic: The Dhar Commission was constituted in 1948 — this is the first formal inquiry post-independence: must come first.
The JVP Committee was constituted in 1949, following the Dhar Commission's report: second.
The SRC (Fazl Ali Commission) was constituted in 1953, after Potti Sriramulu's death forced the political situation: third.
The States Reorganisation Act 1956 implemented (modified) SRC recommendations: fourth and last. Correct sequence: 2-4-1-3, corresponding to option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap involves the JVP Committee and SRC — students who recall the political salience of JVP (Nehru-Patel-Sitaramayya) may place it after the SRC, not realising the SRC came four years after the JVP. The sequence Dhar (1948) → JVP (1949) → SRC (1953) → SRA (1956) is a clean four-step timeline that UPSC can shuffle in any order.
solution.final_explanation:
Four milestones mark the path from initial inquiry to final legislation on linguistic reorganisation:

1. Dhar Commission (1948): First formal inquiry; recommended administrative efficiency over linguistic basis.
2. JVP Committee (1949): Conditional deferral by political leadership; left door open.
3. States Reorganisation Commission (Fazl Ali, 1953–55): Comprehensive multi-factor review triggered by Potti Sriramulu's death and Andhra State's formation.
4. States Reorganisation Act 1956: Legislative culmination implementing (modified) SRC recommendations.

— Placing JVP before Dhar (both reject linguistic basis, but Dhar was 1948, JVP was 1949)
— Placing SRC before the JVP (SRC was 1953, four years after JVP)
— Placing SRA before SRC (the Act implemented the Commission's report)

Value Addition:
• Potti Sriramulu's death (December 1952) is the political hinge between JVP's conditional deferral and the SRC's constitution.
• The SRC submitted its report in October 1955; the SRA was enacted on 31 August 1956 and took effect on 1 November 1956.

solution.concept_anchor: Punjab 1966 — SRC rejection of Punjabi Suba contradicted by 1966 Act

statement_analysis.statement: The States Reorganisation Commission (SRC) 1955 had recommended the bifurcation of Punjab into a Punjabi-speaking state and a Hindi-speaking state.
statement_analysis.reason: The SRC explicitly rejected the demand for Punjabi Suba — the bifurcation of Punjab along linguistic lines. The 1966 reorganisation thus directly contradicted the SRC's 1955 recommendation.

statement_analysis.statement: Chandigarh was designated as a Union Territory serving as the shared capital of both Punjab and Haryana after the 1966 reorganisation.
statement_analysis.reason: Following the Punjab Reorganisation Act 1966, Chandigarh was made a Union Territory and designated as the shared capital of the newly formed Punjab and Haryana — a deliberate political compromise that persists to this day.

statement_analysis.statement: The Shah Commission (1966) recommended the bifurcation of Punjab into Punjabi-speaking Punjab and Hindi-speaking Haryana.
statement_analysis.reason: The Shah Commission was constituted to determine which areas should form the new Punjab and which should form Haryana; its recommendation of bifurcation was implemented by the Punjab Reorganisation Act 1966.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who recall 'SRC supported Punjabi Suba' will mark Statement 1 as correct and look for other incorrect statements, potentially misidentifying Statement 2 or 3.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1 — 'SRC recommended bifurcation of Punjab': this is factually inverted; SRC rejected Punjabi Suba demand: Statement 1 is INCORRECT.
Evaluate Statement 2 — 'Chandigarh as shared Union Territory capital of Punjab and Haryana': established fact, still operative: Correct.
Evaluate Statement 3 — 'Shah Commission recommended bifurcation into Punjab and Haryana': documented mandate and outcome: Correct.
Only Statement 1 is not correct — select option (a): 1 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap in Statement 1 asserts the SRC 'recommended bifurcation of Punjab' — the opposite of what it actually did. Students who know 'there were two events — SRC 1956 and Punjab Reorganisation 1966 — and they both involve Punjab' may assume continuity of recommendation rather than contradiction. The critical UPSC-tested fact is that 1966 contradicted 1956 on Punjab.
solution.final_explanation:
Punjab's reorganisation in 1966 is a landmark case of a post-SRC reorganisation that directly contradicted the SRC's own findings.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The SRC 1955 explicitly rejected the Punjabi Suba demand. The 1966 Punjab Reorganisation Act created Punjabi Suba despite (not because of) the SRC's position — a clear reversal.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Chandigarh's status as a shared Union Territory capital for Punjab and Haryana is an enduring political compromise. Punjab has historically demanded full control of Chandigarh.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The Shah Commission (also known as the Boundary Commission) was specifically tasked with delineating the boundaries between the proposed Punjab and Haryana.

Value Addition:
• The Akali Dal's demand was officially framed as linguistic (Punjabi language in Gurmukhi script) to distinguish it from a religious demand — but the Sikh majority dimension was widely acknowledged.
• Haryana became a predominantly Hindi-speaking state; the hill districts went to Himachal Pradesh.
• Punjab's demand for Chandigarh remains an unresolved inter-state issue — a live example of the 1956 reorganisation's incomplete political settlements.

solution.concept_anchor: Telangana 2014 — bifurcation of linguistically homogeneous state, Article 3 override
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who recall 'Telangana was part of Hyderabad state before 1956' may choose option (b), attributing its distinctiveness to its pre-independence administrative history rather than to its sub-regional identity within a linguistically unified post-1956 state.
elimination_logic: The scenario involves a state seeking separation from a linguistically homogeneous larger state — the parent state government opposes separation but Parliament proceeds: this maps to Telangana 2014.

Eliminate option (a) — the linguistic basis was the justification for MERGING Telangana with Andhra in 1956, not for separating it in 2014. The 2014 logic was sub-regional identity, not a new linguistic argument.
Eliminate option (b) — pre-1956 administrative history (Hyderabad state) is contextual background, not the constitutional principle applied in 2014.
Eliminate option (d) — tribal/ethnic basis (as in Nagaland) was not the operative principle for Telangana; it was sub-regional cultural and developmental identity within a Telugu-speaking majority.

Retain option (c) — the 2014 bifurcation demonstrated that Parliament's power under Article 3 allows separation even of linguistically homogeneous states on sub-regional identity and developmental grounds, overriding the 1956 merger logic.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap: option (a) uses 'linguistic basis' — which was central to 1956 — and applies it to 2014, making it sound plausible. But the 2014 bifurcation was the opposite: it split a linguistically homogeneous Telugu-speaking state, meaning linguistic unity was no longer sufficient to prevent separation. The principle applied in 2014 was sub-regional historical-cultural and developmental distinctiveness.
solution.final_explanation:
The scenario describes the creation of Telangana in 2014 — India's 29th state.

The key principle being tested: Parliament used Article 3 to bifurcate Andhra Pradesh despite the state legislature passing a resolution against bifurcation and despite both new states sharing the Telugu language.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The 2014 bifurcation was NOT based on linguistic distinctiveness — both Telugu-speaking Andhra Pradesh and Telangana share the same language. This directly inverts the 1956 merger logic where linguistic unity justified merger.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: While Telangana's pre-1956 history as part of Hyderabad state is relevant context, it was not the constitutional principle applied in 2014 for bifurcation.
• Option (c) — Correct: The 2014 case established that Parliament's Article 3 power is broad enough to bifurcate even a linguistically homogeneous state on the grounds of sub-regional historical, cultural, and developmental identity — explicitly departing from the 1956 logic.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Tribal/ethnic basis (as with Nagaland 1963) was not the rationale for Telangana; it was sub-regional identity and development grievances within a linguistically unified Telugu-speaking population.

Value Addition:
• The Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act 2014 made Hyderabad a shared capital for up to 10 years, creating an unprecedented shared-capital arrangement.
• The Telangana case is the first instance of bifurcating a linguistically homogeneous state in post-independence India.
• The failure of the Gentlemen's Agreement (1956) to protect Telangana's interests is the direct historical causation for the 2014 separation.

solution.concept_anchor: 7th Amendment and SRA 1956 — simultaneous operation on 1 November 1956

statement_analysis.statement: The 7th Constitutional Amendment Act 1956 abolished the distinction between Part A, Part B, Part C, and Part D states and created a binary classification of States and Union Territories.
statement_analysis.reason: The 7th Amendment, enacted alongside the SRA, abolished the four-part classification and replaced it with the binary of States and Union Territories — a fundamental restructuring of India's federal architecture.

statement_analysis.statement: The 7th Constitutional Amendment Act and the States Reorganisation Act 1956 came into force on different dates — the Amendment preceded the Act by six months to prepare the constitutional ground for reorganisation.
statement_analysis.reason: Both the 7th Constitutional Amendment and the States Reorganisation Act came into force simultaneously on 1 November 1956 — there was no six-month gap between them.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) (both correct) is strongly deceptive because the logical sequence (amendment first, then Act) seems natural — why would Parliament not prepare the constitutional ground before passing the reorganisation Act?
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1 — 7th Amendment abolished the Part A/B/C/D classification and created States/Union Territories binary: established constitutional history: Correct.
Interrogate Statement 2 — 'came into force on different dates, six months apart': this is factually wrong. Both instruments came into force on 1 November 1956 simultaneously: Incorrect.
Statement 1 Correct + Statement 2 Incorrect → option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap fabricates a six-month gap between the 7th Amendment and the SRA. Students who think constitutionally — 'you amend first, then legislate' — will accept that the Amendment preceded the Act. In reality, both came into force simultaneously on 1 November 1956, which is why November 1 is celebrated as statehood day across Karnataka, Kerala, Andhra Pradesh, and other states formed that day.
solution.final_explanation:
The 7th Constitutional Amendment and the States Reorganisation Act 1956 are two instruments of the same constitutional moment.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The 7th Amendment abolished the four-part classification (Part A, B, C, D) that had reflected the pre-integration diversity of British provinces and princely states, replacing it with the simpler binary of States and Union Territories.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Both instruments came into force on the same date — 1 November 1956. There was no preparatory six-month gap. The simultaneity of their operation is a key fact, as they were complementary instruments: the Amendment provided constitutional authority; the Act implemented the territorial reorganisation.

Value Addition:
• 1 November 1956 is Karnataka Rajyotsava (Statehood Day), Kerala Piravi (birth of Kerala), and is significant across multiple southern states.
• The Rajpramukhs of former princely states were replaced by Governors on 1 November 1956 — a critical democratic uniformity milestone.
• Part D had only one entity — Andaman and Nicobar Islands — which became a Union Territory.

solution.concept_anchor: Nagaland 1963 — first state on ethnic/tribal basis, 16th state
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know 'North-East states were formed in 1972' may select Meghalaya, forgetting that Nagaland preceded the 1972 batch by nearly a decade as the first tribal-identity-based state.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a) — Meghalaya was formed in 1972, not 1963; it followed Nagaland's ethnic template but was not the first.
Eliminate option (b) — Manipur was also made a full state in 1972, not the first tribal/ethnic-basis state.
Retain option (c) — Nagaland was formed on 1 December 1963 as India's 16th state, specifically on the basis of Naga tribal identity — the first ethnic/tribal-basis state.
Eliminate option (d) — Tripura became a full state in 1972; it is also not the first ethnic-basis state.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap conflates Nagaland (1963) with the 1972 North-East batch (Meghalaya, Manipur, Tripura). Students who recall 'North-East states have tribal/ethnic basis' without distinguishing Nagaland's 1963 precedence from the 1972 states will select Meghalaya or Manipur. Nagaland's 1963 date makes it the deliberate, first exception to the 1956 linguistic principle.
solution.final_explanation:
The first state formed on ethnic/tribal rather than linguistic grounds tests precision of both the identity and the year.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Meghalaya was formed in 1972, nine years after Nagaland, on ethnic/tribal grounds (Khasi, Garo, Jaintia communities).
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Manipur became a full state in 1972; it was a Union Territory before that.
• Option (c) — Correct: Nagaland, formed on 1 December 1963, was the first state carved on ethnic/tribal (Naga tribal) identity, deliberately departing from the 1956 linguistic principle.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Tripura became a full state in 1972, not the first ethnic-basis state.

Value Addition:
• Nagaland's statehood was preceded by the 16-Point Agreement (1960) between the Government of India and the Naga People's Convention.
• Nagaland's creation acknowledged that the 1956 linguistic principle had limits — tribal identity was a legitimate and separate basis.
• The 1963 precedent paved the way for the broader North-East reorganisation of 1972.

solution.concept_anchor: Samyukta Maharashtra vs Mahagujarat — correct attribution of movements
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who vaguely know 'there was a Gujarat movement for Bombay city' may associate Mahagujarat with a claim for Bombay city as their capital, when actually Bombay city was disputed but ultimately went to Maharashtra.
elimination_logic: Evaluate option (a) — Mahagujarat Movement sought a separate Gujarati state, NOT specifically claiming Bombay city for Gujarat; the Bombay city question was disputed but resolved in Maharashtra's favour: Incorrect pairing.
Evaluate option (b) — Samyukta Maharashtra Movement agitated for a unified Marathi-speaking state including Bombay city; Bombay ultimately became part of Maharashtra: Correct pairing.
Evaluate option (c) — The SRC recommended a bilingual Bombay state, not bifurcation into Maharashtra and Gujarat; bifurcation came in 1960 after the agitations: Incorrect pairing.
Evaluate option (d) — Bombay Reorganisation Act was 1960, not 1956; 1956 retained bilingual Bombay: Incorrect pairing.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap in option (a) attributes to the Mahagujarat Movement a claim for Bombay city for Gujarat — when actually Bombay city was the crux of the Samyukta Maharashtra demand. The Mahagujarat Movement sought a separate Gujarati state, with Ahmedabad as its natural capital. The dispute over Bombay city's inclusion was between Maharashtra's aspirations and the SRC's bilingual proposal, not between the two movements symmetrically.
solution.final_explanation:
The Bombay agitations are a paired-movement testing scenario where students must attribute the correct demand to the correct movement.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The Mahagujarat Movement sought a separate Gujarati-speaking state, not specifically a claim over Bombay city. Bombay city ultimately went to Maharashtra.
• Option (b) — Correct: The Samyukta Maharashtra Movement agitated for a unified Marathi-speaking state that included Bombay city, which was initially proposed as a separate Union Territory. The movement succeeded — Bombay (Mumbai) became part of Maharashtra under the 1960 Act.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The SRC (Fazl Ali Commission) recommended retaining Bombay as a bilingual state — it did NOT recommend bifurcation. Bifurcation came through the 1960 Act after the agitations.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The Bombay Reorganisation Act was enacted in 1960, not 1956. The 1956 SRA retained a bilingual Bombay.

Value Addition:
• Maharashtra Day and Gujarat Day (1 May) commemorate the 1960 bifurcation — both communities celebrate the same date as founding moments.
• The Bombay city question was the most politically charged element of the entire western India reorganisation.
• The SRC's bilingual Bombay proposal is the clearest example of the Commission's failure to anticipate mass political resistance.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 3 — ordinary legislation, consultation not concurrence

statement_analysis.statement: Under Article 3 of the Constitution, Parliament may diminish the area of a state or alter its boundaries by passing a bill with a simple majority, without requiring the concurrence of the state legislature whose territory is affected.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 3 empowers Parliament to reorganise states through ordinary legislation. The state legislature is entitled only to consultation (not concurrence), and Parliament can override the state's views — demonstrated by Telangana's creation despite Andhra Pradesh's opposition.

statement_analysis.statement: Any reorganisation of states under Article 3 constitutes an amendment to the Constitution and therefore requires a special majority in Parliament under Article 368.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 4 of the Constitution explicitly states that laws made under Article 3 shall not be deemed to be amendments of the Constitution — such laws are passed by simple majority, making this statement incorrect.

statement_analysis.statement: The state legislature referred to in Article 3's consultation requirement has the power to veto the proposed reorganisation by passing a resolution against the bill.
statement_analysis.reason: The state legislature's role under Article 3 is consultative only — Parliament is not bound by the state legislature's resolution, as demonstrated by the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act 2014 where Parliament overrode the negative resolution of the Andhra Pradesh legislature.

solution.strong_distractor: d — All three correct is the strongest distractor; Statement 2 uses sophisticated constitutional language ('amendment under Article 368') that sounds authoritative, and Statement 3 uses 'veto power' which aligns with a common misconception about federal consent requirements.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1 — Article 3 allows reorganisation by ordinary (simple majority) legislation, consultation only required: Correct.
Interrogate Statement 2 — Article 4 explicitly says Article 3 laws are NOT constitutional amendments under Article 368: Incorrect.
Interrogate Statement 3 — 'veto power' is the trap phrase; state legislature can pass a resolution but Parliament can proceed regardless: Incorrect.
Only Statement 1 correct — select option (a): 1 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Two scope-extension traps operate simultaneously. Statement 2 extends 'constitutional significance' into 'constitutional amendment requirement' — ignoring Article 4's explicit provision that Article 3 laws are not amendments. Statement 3 extends 'consultation requirement' into 'veto power' — ignoring that Parliament can override state opinion. Both traps exploit the intuition that federal systems require state consent for territorial changes.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 3, read with Article 4, creates a unique constitutional arrangement for state reorganisation.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 3 allows Parliament to form new states, alter boundaries, diminish areas, and change names through ordinary legislation (simple majority). The affected state legislature must be consulted, not concurred with.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Article 4 explicitly states that a law under Article 3 shall not be deemed an amendment of the Constitution under Article 368. This is why reorganisation requires no special majority.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The state legislature's resolution is advisory, not binding. Telangana's creation (2014) is the definitive illustration — Andhra Pradesh's negative resolution was overridden.

Value Addition:
• Article 3 begins with: 'Parliament may by law...' — the phrase 'by law' (not 'by constitutional amendment') is itself the textual basis for ordinary majority sufficiency.
• No state's geographical integrity is constitutionally guaranteed in India — a significant contrast with many federal constitutions worldwide.
• The Babulal Parate case (1960) is the judicial authority confirming Parliament's plenary power under Article 3.
